stem:
Ramesha is a previously healthy 5-month-old girl who presents with a 3-day history of runny nose and cough. Today her parents are concerned that she has been breathing fast and not feeding. On examination, she has a temperature of 37°C, oxygen saturation of 96% on room air, moderate increased work of breathing with tachypnea, and soft wheeze throughout her chest. You diagnose bronchiolitis.

Ramesha's parents ask whether anything can be done to prevent asthma. Which of the following points about asthma prevention is supported by available evidence?

options.text: Avoidance of environmental tobacco exposure may reduce childhood asthma
Breast feeding is recommended to reduce the risk of asthma
If not receiving breast milk, hydrolysed milk formula may reduce childhood asthma and allergy, compared to other formulas
Omega-3-fatty acid supplementation, probiotic supplementation and soy formula may reduce the risk of childhood asthma
Avoidance of common food allergens (such as peanut, egg, and seafood) during pregnancy, breast feeding and infant diets may reduce the risk of childhood asthma
There are no ways of reducing the risk of childhood asthma

explanation: Avoiding environmental tobacco smoke exposure is associated with reduced risk of childhood asthma. The other listed strategies have not been shown reliably to prevent asthma.

citations.title: Practice Quiz: Asthma Management: Medications and Devices - Part B

rationale: This is a single-best-answer item asking about evidence-based asthma prevention. Among the options, avoidance of environmental tobacco exposure is the best-supported measure.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Exposure to environmental tobacco smoke is a modifiable risk factor for childhood asthma.
optionExplanations.B: Breastfeeding has many benefits, but evidence that it prevents asthma is inconsistent and not strong enough to recommend for this purpose alone.
optionExplanations.C: Hydrolysed formulas have not been shown consistently to prevent childhood asthma or allergy.
optionExplanations.D: These interventions are not established asthma-prevention strategies.
optionExplanations.E: Routine avoidance of common allergens during pregnancy, breastfeeding, or infancy does not prevent asthma and is not recommended for this purpose.
optionExplanations.F: Incorrect because some modifiable exposures, such as tobacco smoke, may reduce asthma risk when avoided.
